title: A listener grabbed my arm in the middle of a Vienna event and said, “I know your voice.” I took a selfie and posted it, thrilled. Hours later, my first real fan moment turned into my first real…

blocks.text: The second episode of the history podcast talk brought three podcasters together for a conversation about their work, their struggles, and the strange ways the past keeps showing up in the present. Kati, who tells the stories of Austria and works as a city guide in Vienna, explained that she actually started as a YouTuber before anything else. “I was a student who was annoyed that there wasn’t enough solid material about my subject on YouTube,” she said. “So I made it myself.

Then, after my studies, I became a city guide, which was completely different, and I fell in love with the job. That’s when I decided to bring it all together and make a channel about Austrian history. ”

Her tours range from the classic sights to the morbid corners of Vienna. “We do cemetery tours, crypt tours, everything macabre. It works great here,” she laughed. “And many of my followers book me because of my focus on women’s history. There are plenty of Habsburg women to talk about. ” Jonas, who tells the history of Germany from 1933 to 1945, admitted he had never been recognized by a listener.

“I live in a village. The people who listen to my podcast, I already knew them before,” he said. Kati, however, had recently met a fan for the first time. “I was at an event and this nice guy came up to me and said, ‘I know your voice, I listen to your podcast all the time. ’ I was so surprised I took a selfie immediately and posted it online. That was my first real listener. ” Jonas explained that he used to be a teacher but quit after a few years. “The podcast only became possible because I stopped teaching.

But actually, the motivation to tell history as a continuous story comes from school. I always found it frustrating that we couldn’t follow the connections properly. I used to try to build little narratives into my lessons, but in the classroom you’re not there to entertain people and then quiz them. I felt that format was missing, especially for the Nazi period. Working chronologically helped me understand it better myself, and I learn something new with every piece of research. ” Kati nodded. “I can really relate to that. The research isn’t the hard part.

There’s so much material, especially digital sources, regional histories, even stories of individual people. The problem is selecting and organizing everything. That’s the real challenge. ” She was currently working on Crown Prince Rudolf. “There’s everything from serious scholarship to endless conspiracy theories, stories about his alleged lover, it’s a bottomless pit. I’m seriously considering how many episodes I’ll have to split this into. ” For her own work, she had shifted to a chronological approach. “I stumbled into it.

At first I just made things I found interesting, but now I’m building the history of the Habsburgs in order. I found Emperor Franz Joseph’s diaries, and through them the diaries of his brothers, and then there are cross references to other family members. When I found the diaries, I got hooked. I want diaries and letters that are as close to reality as possible. I don’t want to make the hundredth Habsburg video telling the same stories as everyone else. I want to bring the people closer, and you can only do that through their own written words. ” Jonas held up a book. “This is Hjalmar Schacht.

I love autobiographies and diaries. He was the Reichsbank president under Hitler and later the economics minister. He brought in the billions that built the German tanks and planes, and later in Nuremberg he didn’t want to know anything about it. The guy has incredible charisma and writes extremely well. When you read his autobiography, you catch yourself thinking he’s cool, which is awful. ” He also mentioned Victor Klemperer’s diaries. “They’re fascinating but absolute time eaters. ” Jonas explained that his approach was simpler because he started in the early Middle Ages.

“There aren’t many autobiographies from that period. I rely mostly on secondary literature and give myself an overview. But I still need more than just an overview. I need particularities, stories. Since I always have a guest, the conversation only works if I already know what every answer could be. When something different comes, it’s even better because it surprises me. I go to the university library in Hamburg and borrow the five main works on the topic. I read one properly and skim the rest. Before starting the podcast, I also traveled around Germany and visited many sites. Being there in person makes a huge difference. When I was in Vienna recently, I finally understood how the Ringstrasse worked, that the city wall used to be there and the glacis in front of it gave them open shooting range. I need to see places to really understand them, and local guides always tell different stories than the standard books.

” When asked how he found his guests, he laughed. “At the beginning, I was terrified. I’m not a historian, I studied law, I was a journalist, I’d never made a podcast, and I had zero listeners. Why would anyone talk to me? So I approached a junior professor in Hamburg and asked if we could make a pilot. She had taught a seminar about podcasting. She told me not to worry, that academics are all state funded and happy to talk about their work. And she was right.

It also helps when you get a prominent name. When Professor Schneidmüller, a well-known medieval historian who appears on TV, agreed to come on, that changed things. After that, I could write to other experts and say, ‘Professor Schneidmüller suggested I contact you. ’ That’s the perfect introduction. ” Kati told him he was underselling himself. “Schneidmüller is premier league, and you got him. ” Jonas smiled. “He was incredibly kind and supportive.

Now I ask him for advice on every topic, and he recommends people. The guests are all different. Some sit down and freely answer, and it turns out great. Others write out every word and read it. I try to ask extra questions they didn’t expect so it doesn’t sound too rehearsed. They’re professionals, though, and can deliver a text as if they just came up with the idea. Then it’s up to the editing, which sometimes takes two days, to bring out the human instead of the professorial. ” Kati, who came from academia, appreciated that.

“I’m actually an early modern historian by training, but I never studied the Nazi period. That was always my private passion, my evening reading. In academia, people are genuinely happy to talk at a different level, a freer level. When it’s staged for TV, it’s all scripted and stiff. You spend five hours in a cold church for five minutes of footage. It’s a performance of expertise rather than a real conversation. And where else do historians appear nowadays? It’s a rare exception. So what you’re doing is a great service. ”

Jonas asked about the guests he had lined up. “I’ve recorded up to Charles V now. I talked about Luther and then with Heinz Schilling about Charles V. Next are witch trials and counter reformation, then the Thirty Years’ War. ” Kati mentioned her doctoral supervisor had written a biography of Maria Theresa. Jonas brightened. “Then I’m already meeting with her.
I’ll have to tell her you send your regards. ” He looked for recommendations on witch trials. Kati suggested her doctoral father, Peter Oestmann, a legal historian. Jonas wrote it down.

“I’ll meet him personally, then we can have a drink together. ” He admitted he had initially wanted to talk only with female scholars. “I didn’t want to become another old white man podcast. But the junior professor talked me out of it. She said it’s an honorable intention, but I should have the best person for each topic and not let the gender question dominate completely. That made sense. Still, I always ask for women first. Recently I had three male guests in a row, so for the witch trials it would be great to have a woman, and I already have one.

But I still like collecting names. Peter Oestmann, noted. ” The conversation turned to Kati’s first YouTube shitstorm, which came after she made a video about Andreas Hofer, the Tyrolean freedom fighter. She took a breath. “I was born in Tyrol, although commenters on the video tried to deny that too, because apparently they thought nobody from Tyrol could say what I said. So here’s the story. In 1809, Tyrol belonged to Bavaria. Napoleon’s wars had gone badly for the Habsburgs, they kept losing territory, and Tyrol was handed to the Bavarians, who were the French allies.

For a few years, that wasn’t a problem. But then Vienna thought, maybe we can strike against Napoleon again, and the Tyroleans are unhappy anyway. The Bavarians had brought a lot of Enlightenment reforms, opening markets, restricting religious holidays, even vaccinations. That didn’t sit well with the deeply religious rural population. Many people felt they were ruled by foreigners. So Andreas Hofer stepped forward. He stood out because he could read, unlike many people back then. He was a trader and innkeeper, spoke several languages, had been in fights before, and had a beard. He was a man people trusted. They rose up under his leadership and threw the Bavarians out, and those three battles around Innsbruck have been completely mythologized. Afterwards, Hofer briefly became the ruler of the land, though he didn’t want the job. He wasn’t a politician, but there was nobody else.

What followed was very backwards. If I may bring in the women’s perspective, he actually decreed that women showing a bit more cleavage could be publicly punished by anyone. And I do mean anyone. So yes, Taliban of Tyrol. At the same time, he had some decent ideas which were fine for his era. But you can’t sugarcoat it. There were Jews who were thrown out of the capital, there was looting, and university professors were expelled. Some people openly said they would have preferred the Bavarians to stay. But those voices are never heard. The story told is always the great freedom hero who stood up, motivated the people, and kicked out the Bavarians and the French. ”

She continued. “Then the enemy regrouped, sent new troops, and defeated the main Austrian army. Napoleon stood in Vienna and pressured the emperor, who kept the Tyroleans waiting until the very end, hoping he could still turn things around. The Tyroleans trusted the emperor completely. Their motto was ‘for God, Emperor, and Fatherland. ’ In the end, the emperor simply dropped them and handed Tyrol back to Bavaria. That was a hard blow. Andreas Hofer couldn’t believe it. He withdrew and fled across the border, which wasn’t a border then, to South Tyrol, because at that time it was all one Tyrol. He went into hiding, and a bounty was placed on his head.

The fighting continued because people refused to believe the emperor had abandoned them. Napoleon warned that anyone found with a weapon would be shot. Hofer still said, keep fighting. Looking at it today, those were senseless sacrifices. He was finally betrayed by the so-called Judas of Tyrol, a man named Franz Raffl, who took his silver and handed Hofer to the French. Hofer was taken to Mantua and executed. Later, he was dug up, brought back to Tyrol, given a huge memorial and a magnificent tomb in the Hofkirche. And since then, depending on which ruler was in charge, he’s been wildly instrumentalized. Under the Nazis, he was suddenly turned into a German hero, which is completely absurd because he fought against German and Bavarian rule. Today, he’s an untouchable figure. The Tyrolean anthem is a song about his death. It’s the only Austrian state anthem that doesn’t praise the beauty of the land or its people, but mourns a martyr.

From today’s perspective, at the very least, that’s worth discussing. ” The video, almost two hours long, addressed some of the negative sides for once. “I got a real shitstorm,” she said. “People called me an ultraleft feminist, they said I must be German, which is the worst insult you can get in Austria, they called me a traitor to the country. They couldn’t stand that anyone would tell the story from a more critical perspective. I watched my own video again because I couldn’t believe it. I never said Hofer was a horrible figure who should be erased from the history books. I just also mentioned negative things.

And that was apparently unacceptable. I started wondering what such a figure who lived two hundred years ago means to people personally, and why saying something negative about him feels like a knife in their own heart. ” Jonas asked how she handled it. “I’m very emotional. I can’t just let it slide, even though people advise me to. I replied to every single comment. I argued with people who told me to read a real book and stop spreading fake news. I was like, excuse me, at the beginning of the video I listed a whole bibliography and thanked museum directors who had personally guided me through the exhibitions.

These Hofer cultists clearly haven’t been to a museum or read a book about him in a long time. When I pointed out the bibliography, they said they wouldn’t click the video again so I could game the algorithm. It was insane. Some even went into other people’s positive comments and told them not to trust me. ” Jonas said he recognized the pattern. “On Spotify, my comments are usually constructive, and you can have real discussions. On YouTube, it’s different. I keep getting the same comments under the Nazi videos.

‘The Nazis were left wing,’ or something about the current government. I’m fairly sure the people writing that haven’t watched the video. It’s simply impossible. But I recently had a good discussion with someone who wrote a long response to my episode on the Reich concordat between the Nazi regime and the Catholic Church, listing everything he claimed was factually wrong. I politely asked if he could give me some literature, because in every episode description I quote the best sources I used so people can verify. He actually sent me titles. I responded and classified them for other readers. It helps to be a historian yourself because you often know these works. After that, he said he’d send me his own essay when it was done. We were a hundred percent apart, but we discussed at eye level. That’s how it should be. I always think about the silent readers in these threads.

If someone praises my work and someone else attacks it, the negative comment just stands there unless I respond. I don’t know how much it accomplishes, but I do it for the people reading along. ” Kati asked Jonas whether his topic didn’t depress him. He was currently in 1935, with ten more years ahead, and things only got worse. He paused and explained. “It’s a good question. Let me answer by telling you how I got there. I was always interested in the Nazi period, but I never studied it.

The main reason was that I thought if I specialized in it, I would have to deal with this miserable era for the rest of my life, human suffering on so many levels and in such detail. So I never did. I learned about it privately, through family history. I knew my great grandmother and talked with her for many years. She was a young woman during the Nazi era. My maternal grandparents, my grandmother I was able to interview, was just twelve or thirteen when the war ended. That was my engagement, my interest. It was personal. And that’s why I could handle those horrible stories. I’m a rather sensitive and empathetic person, they say, and it affects me deeply. But on that family level, it made sense. When I started the podcast, it was out of the need to bring this period to people chronologically, because I feel we’re all looking for orientation, and all we get are fragments, episodes.

I was worried it would eventually become too much for me. But the opposite happened. The more detailed I get, and the more episodes I make, the better I feel. Because now I finally understand all those small stories of resistance, and the personal depths of the perpetrators and bystanders. It makes it more tangible and, strangely, less terrible. I can handle it now. I worked a lot with the Reinhard Heydrich biography. He was such a terribly banal person. That aura of evil disappears. ”

Kati said she had recently listened to that episode. “It was fascinating that his wife Lina was actually the political one in the relationship, and he was originally unpolitical, and she politicized him. ” Jonas nodded. “Absolutely. That surprised me too. The photo we all know is Nazi propaganda, he really looks like an Aryan demigod. But when you see private photos, it looks different. Lina was the Nazi connection, her father was a party judge and high official. Heydrich himself was nationally minded, wanted to join the First World War but had bad timing, then joined the Freikorps but was too young, then the navy seeking adventure, and he became a radio operator. He met Lina while already engaged, and she introduced him to ideology and political thinking. He may have been nationally minded, but whether he had been an antisemite before, nobody really knows.

He learned all that from her. Then he was thrown out of the navy over some stupid affair, and through her connections he got a job interview with Heinrich Himmler. Himmler thought Heydrich was an intelligence officer, but he had only been a radio operator, so it was a misunderstanding. Heydrich traveled to Munich and sat down with Himmler, and Himmler was impressed. I don’t want to psychoanalyze, but the tall blond man stood there in a sharp suit, and they talked. Heydrich realized Himmler thought he was an intelligence officer, so he didn’t correct him and just sketched out an entire security service for the SS, using knowledge he had gathered from spy novels he read as a youth. You can read all that in Gerwarth’s biography. It brings it closer, because history is full of myths, and this demythologizes it completely. ”

Kati admitted she had been hesitant about Jonas’s podcast. “I had circled around it because I wondered if I really wanted to engage with that period in such detail. After three or four episodes, I was completely hooked. It had exactly that effect on me. It didn’t make things more sympathetic, but it made them more graspable. ” Jonas asked Kati whether she had answers about the Andreas Hofer reaction. She reflected. “It’s really about identity.

The Tyroleans see themselves through this story of standing apart. We are who we are, and we’re better than everyone else. They don’t say it, but it’s there. You don’t need outsiders coming across the mountains. The horizon is limited, everything is within Tyrol. And I think much of that comes from history. We successfully defended ourselves once because we couldn’t rely on the emperor, we had to take care of ourselves, and then they killed our hero anyway. So we keep him alive forever and reproduce that. There are the Schützen parades, the marksmen who were always responsible for Tyrol’s defense, they march, they shoot into the air, the market women give them schnapps, and you’re not allowed to say anything against it. I find it difficult that women aren’t allowed to participate actively, not just serve drinks. But if you say that, people answer, don’t destroy our traditions. And you think, but traditions grow, they’re not eternal.

Some are even invented. ” Jonas brought up invented traditions like the Cologne carnival and asked his wife, who appeared briefly, when it started. She said 1823. Jonas explained. “The unregulated street carnival was so chaotic that the Prussians were about to ban it. The citizens came together and decided to organize a proper parade, and that’s how the Rosenmontag procession was born. The prince of carnival wasn’t allowed to call himself prince at first, out of fear of offending the Prussian monarchy. The whole thing was really about making fun of the Prussians.

” Kati reflected on deconstruction. “I have the feeling we’re conditioned from school to want everything simple and logical and chronological. First you break things down into neat categories, and later you realize it’s not that simple. The migration period is a great example. It didn’t happen the way it’s usually told. There was no real break between the Roman Empire and the Middle Ages. But those are the stories people love, like Störtebeker, who probably never existed in the way we know him, or Sisi, who was even tattooed, as I recently learned. But when you deconstruct these myths, people get upset because it’s personal.

The Evil Mother-in-Law theme in the Sisi films, for example, that never fails to ignite discussions. In reality, Sophie was initially delighted with Elisabeth and spoke well of her, only the reverse was not the case. But I have to let go of that and say, she wasn’t a dragon, and the other wasn’t a saint. They were both people with light and shadow, like every historical figure. Some people are stuck in their box and you can’t get them out. ” Jonas added that these narrative patterns came from the early days of academic history writing in the nineteenth century. “There’s a scholar named Hayden White who wrote a book called Metahistory. He analyzed how influential historians used certain story patterns.

When you write about the Roman Empire, you use a rise and fall narrative. When you write about the Interregnum, you do the same. And what got lost was presenting people in their full complexity. They were always cast as heroes, antagonists, or Judas figures. That’s where the Judas of Tyrol comes from. History writing comes from writing itself, unlike physics or chemistry. It has only changed massively in recent decades. Maybe now we deconstruct too much for storytelling and reconstruct too little. As podcasters, we can contribute to bringing things back together. ”

Kati agreed. “You have to first explain what the migration period means before you can tell people it didn’t happen that way. You can’t start at the end. We still need these narratives, the question is how to do it better. ” Jonas brought up his own discovery. “I was invited last week to a press conference in Magdeburg, in the university clinic, where they presented the skeleton of Otto the Great. His sarcophagus in the cathedral was in danger of collapsing and had to be restored.

They opened it and removed everything inside. When they took it out, they didn’t know if it was really him. The cathedral had burned down several times, and the remains had been moved for safety and brought back. Nobody knew if the real Otto was still there. The anthropologists examined the skeleton and found a man about 1. 80 meters tall, roughly a thousand years old, with heavily used hip and pelvic muscles indicating he rode a lot. His front teeth were knocked out, his nose bone was displaced, as if he had taken a hard blow to the face. Isotope analysis of his teeth showed he ate fish and meat and no millet, which was poor people’s food. That was luxury nutrition for a thousand years ago. All the clues fit. Then came DNA analysis, but you need a comparison sample. There was no genuine Otto DNA.

However, there was a similar process in Bamberg with his great-nephew, Emperor Henry II, who is also a saint. The church had long been reluctant to allow DNA testing on relics. But the new pope wrote an apostolic letter saying Christian archaeology makes a valuable contribution to the faith, and so the church in Bamberg released a relic bone. Both samples ended up in the same institute in Leipzig. They knew from history that Otto was Henry’s great-uncle, related within three degrees. And exactly that degree of kinship came out in the DNA. If both bones were not genuine, then both would have to have been faked or exchanged in the same degree, which is completely unrealistic. So it’s now almost certain: the relics in Bamberg really are Henry II, and the excellently preserved skeleton in Magdeburg really is the first German-Roman emperor. The best part was that all the scientists stayed after the journalists left. I thought, why should I leave? How often in my life will I have a thousand-year-old emperor lying on a table in front of me? I stayed until the lights went out.

It was the most exciting day of the year for me. ” Kati asked about his new format. Jonas explained he had been thinking for months about the ways history resonates with the present. “The sad occasion was the Iran war. I sat down in front of the camera, made a few bullet points, and just talked, which is the opposite of what I usually do. My scripts are completely written out, with several stages. It worked quite well, though I had to cut a lot. The idea is to put the present under history as a magnifying glass, so the format is called Brennglas.

With the Iran war, I was constantly reminded of the 1930s. Then one morning I had the idea that it reminded me of what happened in Stresa in 1935. Stresa is a resort in northern Italy where Mussolini invited the British and French leaders to discuss how to contain German rearmament. It was a perfectly correct idea. But all that came out of it was a beautiful paper that sounded great. Europe is very good at publishing papers that sound great. Nothing happened because Mussolini himself already had his own imperial ambitions, which he hadn’t communicated honestly to his partners. He wanted a war of conquest in Ethiopia, which was the last non-colonized country in Africa. When he started that war, the British and French objected, though not out of love for freedom and human rights, but because they had their own colonial interests. The point is, all of this was foreseeable. But there was no clear communication and no clear red lines. And the only one who profited was the side that wasn’t even in Stresa: Nazi Germany.

They could keep rearming without consequences. As a bonus, a year later came the Berlin-Rome Axis, because Mussolini thought, if the Western democracies won’t do what I want, I’ll turn to Berlin. I see the same dynamic today. Trump does what he wants, and Europe doesn’t seem to learn that you have to draw clear lines. It worked a bit with Greenland, and half-heartedly with Iran. When the main guarantor of the security order destroys that order himself, you have to learn the lesson: communicate clearly and draw clear lines. Because otherwise alliances break apart, and everyone starts fighting only for themselves. I’m not saying Trump is Hitler, that’s nonsense. But you can learn from dynamics without equating people. History is not a simple lesson, but it’s still a mirror. ”

Kati added a thought. “People often comment, ‘Were you there? Then you can’t talk about it. ’ But if that were true, nobody could talk about history at all, not even those who wrote it. Of course we can only judge from today’s perspective. But I believe people remain the same. Technologies change, systems change, but the dynamics of power and fear and ambition almost never change. You can understand how it might have been back then and think about how it still happens today. ”

The conversation wound down. They agreed that the Brennglas topic alone could fill another two hours, and someone suggested bringing an archetype from the present and a historical counterpart to the next round. They thanked each other, reminded the listeners to subscribe, leave comments, and support all the independent channels. Then the microphones went silent, and the three podcasters went back to their research, their scripts, and the endless work of digging the past out of its myths.
